title: The thirty-hour week
text: The five-day week is a twentieth-century invention; the four-day week may be a twenty-first-century {{1}}. Trials in Iceland, the UK and New Zealand asked companies to {{2}} hours with no cut in pay, and the results have kept {{3}} the argument: most firms reported stable or improved output, lower staff turnover and easier {{4}}. The theory is older than the trials. Working hours {{5}} dramatically in the last century as productivity rose — the eight-hour day was the radical demand of 1886 — and economists have long argued that some of every productivity gain should be {{6}} in time rather than wages. The obstacles are equally well known: manufacturing, healthcare and schools cannot simply {{7}} a day, and managers fear the meetings-and-emails crunch that a short week can produce. The pragmatic verdict so far: it works where the work is {{8}} measured and redesigned, and struggles where presence is mistaken for performance. The direction of travel, though, is unmistakable — we are richer in output than any previous century, and the question is what form the wealth should take.

gaps.explanation: 'may be a twenty-first-century equivalent' — its counterpart from another era; eloquence = fluent speaking.
'asked companies to compress hours' — fit them into fewer days; comprise = consist of.
'results have kept fuelling the argument' — supplying it with energy; foil = thwart.
'lower turnover and easier recruitment' — the process of hiring; recreation = leisure activity.
'working hours fell dramatically' — decreased; the past simple is needed, not the near-forms.
'should be claimed in time rather than wages' — taken as what is owed; acclaim = praise publicly.
'schools cannot simply drop a day' — take it out of the timetable; drape = hang cloth loosely.
'where the work is carefully measured and redesigned' — with attention; carelessly and crudely reverse the meaning.
